newsitem.title: USA: Dole as 'titanic' debater and possible hot author.
newsitem.headline: Dole as 'titanic' debater and possible hot author.

text.p: Bob Dole's skills as an orator got a sardonic nod this week from none other than White House spokesman Mike McCurry as the Republican challenger and the Democratic president prepared to debate.

In detailing President Clinton's campaign schedule, McCurry noted that time would be set aside for preparation for the first presidential debate Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and the second Oct. 16 in San Diego.
His tongue firmly in cheek, McCurry said Clinton hoped to be ready for "this very serious encounter with a titanic juggernaut of a debater."

Dole, famously a man of few words, has joined forces with vice presidential running mate Jack Kemp to produce "Trusting the People," a 164-page book explaining how their plan to cut taxes and balance the federal budget would work.
In bookstores starting Wednesday, the Dole-Kemp campaign tome cites former Presidents John Kennedy and Ronald Reagan in support of the plan.
Paul Olslewski, a spokesman for publisher HarperCollins, said the first printing of the Republicans' book is 200,000 copies but it was too soon to say how well it would sell.
At $15 a copy it is more expensive than a similar-sounding campaign book that came out four years ago -- the 232-page, $7.99 "Putting People First" by then candidates Bill Clinton and Al Gore.

Another 1992 political book is finding new life this week on the Internet: Steve Talley's "Bland Ambition," which recounts the foibles of U.S. vice presidents. Information from the book was used to construct a truly trivial 20-question quiz about the men who have served a heartbeat away from the presidency.

Some sample questions: Which vice president was indicted for murder while in office and was tried for treason after leaving office? Which vice president took three slave wives? Which vice president was sworn in outside the United States and never set foot in Washington during his term?

For answers, go to http://www.catsdogs.com/veepquiz.html. And consider what may be the ultimate vice presidential quote, which is also included in the web site: "My friends, no matter how rough the road may be, we can and we will, never, never surrender to what is right." The speaker was Dan Quayle.

If you had to sum up your impression of the two current vice presidential candidates in one word, what would it be? That question was posed by the Pew Research Centre, which came up with a "Top 20" list for Republican Kemp and Democrat Gore.

Respondents most often thought of Gore as "intelligent," followed by "good," "environmentalist," "honest" and "leadership" -- but lower down on the list were the less-than-flattering "boring," "stiff," "dull," "wimp" and "puppet."
For Kemp, the most frequent association was "football," then "good," "leader," "energetic" and "OK." Unflattering responses got no worse than "unknown."
That was better than Dole's one-word score in a similar poll last month: most respondents thought of him as "old," followed by "good." Clinton's No. 1 word was "good," followed by "wishy-washy."

Speaking of taking the pulse of the voters, one New York congressman may be slightly out of touch. As Congress made a final push to finish its business in advance of the campaign endgame, House Rules Committee chairman Gerald Solomon, a Republican, gave a novel argument for speeding things up: "The people want us out of here. ... They want us back home to campaign in the last five or six weeks of this election."
